name: Confucianism
summary: Confucianism holds that good order comes from moral cultivation, starting in the family, and from virtuous rulers who lead by example, care for the people's livelihood and are served by learned officials. Society is a set of reciprocal role relationships (ruler-subject, parent-child, husband-wife, elder-younger, friend-friend) kept in harmony by ritual. Authority rests on moral rectitude, so a ruler who ceases to be benevolent may lose Heaven's mandate.
scope: Classical Confucianism as set out in the Analects (Confucius) and the Mencius, with the imperial-era and Neo-Confucian tradition as described in reference works. It excludes modern political Confucianism (Jiang Qing, Daniel Bell and others), and Legalist or Xunzi-style variants. Because it is a moral and political philosophy rather than a modern party program, many answers on economic and technological issues are inferred and low-confidence.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Classical texts do not address healthcare, but Mencius makes feeding and caring for the destitute a ruler's first duty, so state-provided care follows by inference.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Mencius wants people to have a secure livelihood but proposes land allocation and light taxes, not wage-setting; adherents have no settled view.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Texts distrust profit-seeking and put righteousness above gain, and Mencius has the ruler arrange livelihoods, though he also wants markets untaxed; inferred skepticism of pure market rule.

public-ownership.rationale: Mencius's well-field system has a common plot beside private ones and the texts never discuss utilities; adherents are split on state ownership.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Mencius demands light taxes on the people and condemns rulers who squeeze them, but does not frame this as taxing the rich; no settled position.

unions-good.rationale: Guilds existed in the tradition but the texts prize harmony under ethical roles, not collective bargaining; no clear position.

property-fundamental.rationale: Mencius treats a stable holding of land as the base of moral order, yet his plan includes a communal plot and ruler duties to redistribute; property is not an absolute right.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Perfectionist politics lets rulers shape the economy for the people's good, so tighter regulation of commerce is inferred as consistent.

cut-welfare.rationale: Caring for the widowed, orphaned and destitute is described as the first act of benevolent government, so cutting relief goes against the texts.

worker-ownership.rationale: Nothing in the texts addresses the structure of enterprise; the tradition honors farmers, artisans and merchants as cooperating occupations without a view on ownership.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Texts favor moral example over coercive control and warn against entrapping people, but also support order; contested and anachronistic.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Confucian ethics stress self-cultivation and moral guidance of the people, so permissive drug policy is inferred as unwelcome.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Rectification of names and ritual propriety value proper speech, but the tradition has no developed view on legal speech limits.

strong-leader.rationale: Rule by a virtuous exemplar is central, but Mencius says a ruler who fails the people may be removed; a strong leader is welcomed only if virtuous.

state-harmful.rationale: Government is the central instrument for moral transformation of the people, so the idea that the state is unnecessary is flatly contrary to the tradition.

limit-guns.rationale: The texts do not address private arms; Mencius prefers moral government to force, but no position on gun law can be drawn.

empower-police-military.rationale: Confucius and Mencius put trust and virtue above force and say conquest without benevolence fails; more coercive authority is not their recipe, though defence is accepted.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Ritual propriety and family-centered ethics make the tradition unfriendly to sex work; inferred rather than stated.

decide-locally.rationale: The texts describe a unified moral kingdom ruled through officials, with no doctrine on subsidiarity; adherents are split.

rehabilitation.rationale: Confucians wanted governments to rely less on penal punishment and more on moral cultivation, and Mencius criticizes punishing people he has failed to provide for.

traditional-family.rationale: Filial piety is the root of virtue and the family is the model of political order; the five relationships centre on family roles.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Lineage continuation and male-line ancestor rites are central to family ethics, so adherents lean against, though the texts say little directly.

abortion-legal.rationale: Continuing the family line is a heavy duty in the tradition, so adherents lean against permissive abortion; not addressed in classical texts.

more-religion-public.rationale: Confucianism has ritual, ancestor veneration and Heaven but no omnipotent deity or church; ritual in public life is valued while a larger role for religion as such is not an issue it takes up.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The tradition has no developed view on race-based redress; it speaks of cultural, not racial, distinctions.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Fixed gender roles in family and ritual are treated as normative, with the husband-wife bond a defined relationship.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Confucius saw himself as transmitting the Zhou cultural heritage, and the tradition prizes continuity of ritual and culture.

gradual-change.rationale: Confucius was a self-described transmitter who valued inherited ritual forms, while allowing reform by virtuous rulers.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Mencius says a benevolent ruler draws people from other states, but there is no doctrine on immigration levels.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The tradition imagines moral order through virtuous kingship, not international bodies; no clear position.

free-trade.rationale: Mencius wants markets and passes untaxed under benevolent rule, but there is no general theory of trade.

nation-first.rationale: Rulers' first duty is to their own people, but the ideal of virtuous rule that attracts others and condemns conquest keeps this from being absolute.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Mencius approves of conquest only when the conquered people welcome it, which resembles a case for liberating intervention, but he also warns against aggression.

open-borders.rationale: Hierarchical, rooted moral community is the base of the tradition; open borders is not its concern and is inferred as unwelcome.

limit-growth.rationale: The texts concern livelihood and virtue; Mencius advises restraint in harvesting, but no doctrine of limiting growth exists.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Not addressed; a virtuous government would care for the people's welfare, but adherents split on the extent of action.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Moral cultivation, not technique, is the tradition's answer to social problems.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Anachronistic and not addressed by any principle.

revolution-justified.rationale: Mencius holds that a ruler who violates benevolence is a mere fellow who may be put to death, and that an evil ruler should be overthrown.

experts-over-public.rationale: The tradition favors rule by the wise and virtuous, selected through learning, over rule by the many; Mencius says those who labor with their minds govern.

central-planning.rationale: Mencius's state arranges land and livelihoods in detail, but the texts never claim planning outperforms markets; inferred mild skepticism.

socialized-markets.rationale: No position on enterprise ownership forms is found in the texts.

land-value-tax.rationale: Mencius favors a light tithe on produce and a well-field system, not a single land-value tax; no stated view on the proposal.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Family continuity and property passing to heirs are valued, but there is no discussion of inheritance tax.

basic-income.rationale: Mencius insists that people be assured a livelihood, but through land and relief for the needy, not an unconditional payment.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Not addressed; Mencius wants border passes untaxed, but this gives no position on modern tariffs.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Mencius gives the ruler an active role in arranging land, schooling and livelihood, from which an activist state economy is inferred.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The well-field ideal gives every family a holding to secure a fixed livelihood and fixed heart, favoring wide distribution of land.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The tradition treats distinct occupations and roles as natural and has no ideal of abolishing exchange.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Anachronistic; the tradition favors government care of the economy, so abolition is inferred as unwelcome.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Hierarchical harmony among occupations sounds corporatist, but the texts do not endorse state-recognized wage bodies.

one-party-rule.rationale: Classical Confucianism has no parties; rule by an educated moral elite is endorsed, and modern Confucian views are split between meritocratic and democratic forms.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Classical Confucianism assumed rule by a virtuous sovereign under the Mandate of Heaven, though legitimacy depends on virtue, not birth alone.

democracy-best.rationale: Classical texts probably contain no idea of democracy but may allow it in some circumstances; modern Confucians split between meritocracy and democracy.

direct-votes.rationale: Policy is meant to be guided by the wise, so direct popular lawmaking is not favored.

workers-councils.rationale: The tradition places authority in educated officials and the ruler, not in class councils.

right-to-secede.rationale: The ideal is a unified moral realm under one virtuous ruler; no right to secede is recognized.

natural-rulers.rationale: The tradition holds that the morally cultivated are suited to rule, and that authority rests on moral rectitude, not might.

political-violence-never.rationale: Mencius justifies killing a tyrant, so political violence is not never justified, though it is a last resort.

war-builds-character.rationale: Confucius and Mencius put virtue and the people's welfare above martial glory, and warn that conquest without benevolence rebounds.

separate-church-state.rationale: Ritual and Heaven are woven into government, but Confucianism has no church to separate from the state.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Government is shaped by ritual and moral teaching drawn from classics, but law as scripture is not the model; rule by virtue and ritual over penal law.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Justice and defence are duties of the virtuous ruler, so private provision runs against the model of government as moral stewardship.

military-superiority.rationale: Mencius advises defence alongside the people, but ranks virtue above arms; no stated view on superiority.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The tradition distinguishes by culture and moral cultivation more than ethnicity, and Mencius says a benevolent ruler draws people from everywhere.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The tradition prizes harmony among hierarchical roles and cooperating occupations, not conflict as the engine of history.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Care for the poor flows from virtue, not from ideals of equality or justice, and hierarchy is normative.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: No position can be drawn from the texts.

civilizational-union.rationale: The tradition imagines a cultural realm radiating from virtue, but not a political union by shared civilization; no clear position.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Righteousness is set against profit; Mencius opens by rejecting talk of profit for benevolence and righteousness.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The tradition stresses cultivating virtue and role duties over enjoying rights, and classical texts lack a rights concept.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Heaven and Earth are revered, but no doctrine of the intrinsic value of nature is stated.

limit-population.rationale: Large families and continuing the male line are central to ancestral duty, so coercive limits are inferred as unwelcome.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Not addressed; the tradition prizes settled civilization and learning, so a rejection of it is unlikely.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Continuity of institutions and ritual is valued over disruptive change.

human-enhancement.rationale: Moral self-cultivation is the route to improvement; anachronistic, inferred skeptical.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Government depends on the virtue and trustworthiness of persons, which algorithms cannot embody; anachronistic.

restore-past-order.rationale: Confucius saw himself as a transmitter of the Zhou heritage and looked back to the sage kings, though he did not oppose all progress.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Policy is meant to flow from moral principle and ritual, so results alone would not be the test.

direct-action.rationale: Reform comes through moral example, learning and advising rulers, with officials remonstrating within the order.

means-match-ends.rationale: Confucius held that rule by example and virtue transforms the people, so methods must embody the order sought.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Civilization, ritual and learning are the basis of the moral order, so foraging is rejected.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Mencius states that those who labor with their minds govern and those who labor with their strength are governed, and calls this a universal principle.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Relief of the destitute is a duty of rulers, but distribution by role and merit is also accepted; no stated principle.

production-for-use.rationale: The texts say little about profit motive in production, beyond condemning profit-seeking by rulers.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The tradition does not use the idea of exploitation; Mencius blames rulers who tax the people excessively, not profit as such.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Confucianism rejects class rule and class conflict, placing authority in the virtuous and educated.

collective-farming.rationale: Mencius's well-field has families farm a common plot together before their own fields, but the farm is not collectivized.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: The tradition locates the causes of war in rulers' lack of virtue and profit-seeking, not in a system; anachronistic.

taxation-theft.rationale: Taxation is legitimate: Mencius debates its form and size (a tithe), not its legitimacy.

harm-principle.rationale: Politics is perfectionist and promotes virtue, opposed to liberal neutrality about the good life.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Persons are defined by role relationships, and classical texts have no concept of individual rights.

conscription.rationale: Mencius is wary of war but accepts defence by ruler and people together; no stated view on conscription.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Mencius notes people leave bad rulers for good ones, but the tradition relies on remonstrance and virtue, not exit, as the check.

state-as-business.rationale: The state is a moral instrument and the ruler a parent of the people, not a business serving customers.

media-academia-power.rationale: Scholars have a role as advisers to rulers, but no stated position on modern media and universities.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Moral ability is attributed to cultivation and education, not to race; Mencius holds human nature as good.

organic-representation.rationale: Family and community are the base of political order, so representation through them is consistent, though the tradition had no such scheme.

total-state.rationale: The ruler shapes culture, education and economy to promote virtue, but the model is moral example and light punishment, not total control.

national-rebirth.rationale: Confucius saw decline from the Zhou and sought restoration, but not a radical rebirth.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Mencius warns that conquest without benevolence is self-defeating and approves taking territory only if the people welcome it.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Loyalty between ruler and minister is central but reciprocal and tied to righteousness; feudal oaths as the base of authority are not endorsed as such.

bound-labor.rationale: Mencius wants farmers secure on their own plots and criticizes exactions that drive them to ruin.

universal-morality.rationale: Heaven is a transcendent moral order and human nature is oriented to virtue, but the tradition does not state a rationalist universalism.

single-common-good.rationale: Politics aims at the people's welfare through virtue, a perfectionist vision of a common good, not the balancing of interests.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Authority by roles and merit is the norm, so democratic voting in firms is not favored.

school-vouchers.rationale: Mencius urges the state to establish schools, but no view on vouchers can be drawn.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Mencius counsels light taxes and frugal rulers, but there is no theory of deficits.

economic-freedom.rationale: Moral order and the ruler's care come first; the texts do not make economic freedom a condition of political freedom.

rule-by-example.rationale: Confucius holds that the ruler's virtue moves the people like wind bending grass, and Confucians wanted far less reliance on penal punishment.

national-self-determination.rationale: Classical Confucianism grounds legitimacy in a ruler's virtue and a civilisational order under Heaven rather than in national identity, so it gives no special claim to a state for each people; this is inferred from the Mandate of Heaven and rule by virtue, since the texts never address nationhood.

force-without-un.rationale: Classical texts do not address the UN, but Confucian politics ties the use of force to moral legitimacy and rulers who win people by virtue rather than arms, so acting on one's own judgment is inferred to be disfavored.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Confucianism grounds right action in ritual, tradition, filial feeling and reverence for Heaven alongside learning, so reason is not treated as the only guide.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Inferred: Mencius makes relief of the destitute a ruler's first duty and says a benevolent ruler draws people from other states, but the texts give no rule on citizens versus newcomers.

positive-liberty.rationale: Confucianism has no notion of freedom as such, but Mencius makes securing the people's livelihood the ruler's first duty, so material means for a decent life are inferred as a public concern.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Mencius puts care for the destitute first yet also expects able people to work their land; the texts do not address welfare conditions, so this is inferred as split.

class-collaboration.rationale: Society is a set of reciprocal roles kept in harmony, and Mencius defends the division between those who rule and those who labour as complementary, not antagonistic.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Confucius presents himself as a transmitter who loves the ancients, and the tradition treats inherited ritual and learning as the basis of order.

dominated-front.rationale: The classical texts have no view on modern Western domination; this is inferred as indifferent, since modern Confucians divide on it.

workers-nation.rationale: Confucianism has no theory of working-class organisation; its units are family, state and all-under-heaven, so the question is inferred as not applicable.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The husband-wife relationship is one of the five defining roles, with different duties for each, and the imperial tradition built this into custom and law.

ban-interest.rationale: Mencius condemns rulers who squeeze the people through heavy exactions, but no source here calls for a legal ban on interest, so this is a weak inference.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Confucian thought distinguishes civilised from barbarian by culture, which can be adopted, rather than by race, so legal racial classification and separation does not follow from it.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The state is a moral order in which a virtuous ruler serves the people, so it is not seen as an instrument of one class.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Texts predate fossil fuels; Mencius cares for the people's livelihood but nothing settles energy supply versus climate, so adherents have no settled view.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: The tradition sees moral and cultural transformation of outsiders through ritual and example (the civilizing ideal), inferred to favor newcomers adopting the dominant culture.

elite-replacement.rationale: Confucian texts hold that disorder comes from rulers' failings, not hidden plots; inferred disbelief in a deliberate elite replacement scheme.

proportional-representation.rationale: Texts say nothing of electoral systems; the stress on rule by the virtuous rather than by parties or majorities gives no clear lean on seat allocation.

national-mission.rationale: The tradition holds that a virtuous ruler's example attracts distant peoples, but it does not urge exporting a political system by mission; split among adherents.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Confucian hierarchy gives men the lead in family and office and scholars note patriarchy in the tradition, so adherents would deny systematic disadvantage to women as a defect needing correction.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Confucians condemn bad rulers and Mencius allows removing them, but they also hold that virtuous officials govern well; no stable view on the political class generally.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: The texts do not address heredity as a policy matter; the emphasis on family continuity and moral cultivation over coercion suggests rejecting state control of procreation.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Mencius allows removing a tyrant, but the texts prize ritual and harmony over punitive justice and never address legal accountability for past abuses.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Mencius and Confucius want rulers to educate, enrich and relieve the people, a far wider role than defence, courts and property.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Classical Confucianism draws the line between civilised and barbarian by culture and moral conduct, not descent, so it has no doctrine of racial separation; this is inferred from that cultural standard.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Mencius holds that human nature is good and anyone can become a sage, an equal moral capacity, yet Confucian order rests on graded roles and status with unequal duties and standing before ritual and law, so adherents are split on the literal claim.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Confucian thought concerns the moral order of one polity and never addresses socialism; the answer is inferred as indifferent.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Classical sources do not address overseas settlement; Mencius judges conquest by whether the people welcome the new ruler, which gives no clear classification, so this is inferred as split.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Imperial law was built around ritual-defined status and kinship rather than religious communities, and the texts do not take up uniform personal law, so the answer is inferred as split.

restrict-conversion.rationale: The classics say nothing on conversion; the imperial state sometimes policed Buddhism and other creeds while generally tolerating a syncretic mix, so adherents are split.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: The texts accept meat in sacrifice and in feeding the aged and show compassion toward animals only as a lesson in feeling, so a legal ban on cattle slaughter is inferred as unlikely.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Confucian education taught the classics with ritual reverence for Heaven and ancestors as part of moral formation, so schools are not expected to be free of such instruction; inferred from that practice.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Mencius advises the small state of Teng, hemmed in by powerful neighbours, to defend itself resolutely but above all to rule virtuously, since moral authority outweighs force; the socialist-state framing does not apply.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Mencius treats the people's welcome as evidence of Heaven's mandate and favours consulting them on key decisions, but legitimacy rests on the ruler's virtue and not on consent as such, so the claim is only partly shared.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Confucians hold that moral truth is knowable through learning and the classics and that learned officials should rule on that basis; the question is modern, so inferred.

trade-surplus.rationale: Classical Confucians looked down on merchants and stressed the people's livelihood over profit, not export balances; inferred.

population-transfer.rationale: Confucian benevolent rule cares for all the people and Mencius condemns harming the people; forced removal contradicts this, though not addressed directly.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Mencius condemns wars of conquest but allows punitive force against tyrants, so adherents would neither accept nor reject an absolute rule.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Confucianism stresses harmony, ritual and reciprocal obligation over struggle, and the Mencius condemns profit-seeking competition.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Parties are modern and the tradition does not address them; adherents would back rulers protecting order but also remonstrance.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Confucians accept hierarchical authority held by virtuous rulers and see reciprocal duties as the check, not freedom from arbitrary power as such; inferred.

separated-powers.rationale: Classical Confucianism relies on the ruler's virtue and moral remonstrance rather than institutional checks; modern Confucians split.

vanguard-party.rationale: Rule by a learned moral elite is Confucian, but a revolutionary party leading workers is not; inferred.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Mencius makes relieving the destitute and securing the people's livelihood a ruler's first duty.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Not addressed; Mencius wants a secure livelihood but proposes no view on selling public housing, and adherents have no settled position.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Inferred from the Confucian priority on social harmony and ordered relationships, which favors limits on disruptive conflict; not directly addressed.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Mencius blames hardship on bad rule, heavy taxes and failure to secure livelihood, not on too many people.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Confucianism is a cultural rather than ethnic doctrine, and adherents are not agreed on diversity; inferred.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Confucian politics is rule by the learned and virtuous, selected by merit and examination, not by chance.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Confucians preferred ritual and moral example to punishment and did not favor suspending legal protections; inferred.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Inferred from Mencius, who makes securing the people's food and livelihood the ruler's first duty.

party-controls-media.rationale: Confucians favor moral guidance by rulers but also valued remonstrance against them; adherents have no settled view.

party-commands-army.rationale: Inferred from Confucian emphasis on rule by the state's virtuous officials, not a party; the question postdates the texts.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Not addressed by the classical texts, and adherents would not agree on a residence period.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Inferred: Mencius ties officials' stipends to rank in a graded hierarchy, which is not an ordinary-wage rule.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Modern parties are not addressed; adherents could favor harmony and unity or distrust factions, so it is left neutral.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Inferred: the tradition looks to a virtuous order for all under Heaven but speaks of no treaty bodies; adherents have no settled view.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The ruler leads by example and appoints learned officials, who may remonstrate but serve him, so executive command sits with the ruler.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Confucianism has no church; inferred from its preference for authority and ritual flowing down from above.

clerical-rule.rationale: Rule by learned moral scholars-officials resembles this, but they are not clergy and the Mandate rests on the ruler's virtue; adherents are split.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Inferred from loyalty owed within the ruler-subject relationship, though Mencius condemns wars of conquest and a tyrant forfeits support.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The tradition holds that ritual, music and learning shape moral character and that the state should promote virtue, as the politics of virtue in the scholarship describes.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Inferred: rulers served without term limits and the test of a ruler was virtue, not tenure.

recall-officials.rationale: Inferred from Mencius, who allows a tyrant to be removed, though by ministers or Heaven's mandate more than by a vote.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Not addressed; Mencius condemns aggressive war and favours benevolent rule, but gives no doctrine on permanent alliances or overseas troops.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Inferred: Mencius wants families to hold allotted land and secure livelihoods, but does not call for banning rental arrangements.

people-in-arms.rationale: Inferred: Mencius condemns war and rule is by learned officials and virtue, so an armed citizenry is not part of the tradition.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Inferred: Mencius builds good government on the farming household and its secure livelihood, so adherents would see rural life as sound.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Inferred: Mencius says the world is settled by a benevolent ruler who unites it, so adherents would favour a divided people being brought together.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Mencius holds that those who labour with their minds govern and those who labour with their strength are governed, and Confucianism prizes learned officials.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Inferred: the tradition distinguishes civilised Chinese ways from outlying ones and holds that others are transformed by them.

death-penalty.rationale: Confucians prefer ritual and moral example to punishment, but the tradition accepted execution for grave crimes; adherents are split.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Inferred: the tradition places sexual morality and the education of the young in the family and its hierarchy, and treats gender roles as differentiated.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Not addressed; Confucianism has no creation doctrine and no stake in how schools teach origins.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Inferred: ritual propriety and moral cultivation lead adherents to support laws against indecency.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Inferred: the family and lineage are the base of Confucian society, so citizenship through family descent fits its emphasis.

minority-language-support.rationale: Inferred: Confucianism stresses a common civilisation and ritual order, so minority languages would not be a priority.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Inferred: order rests on shared ritual and a common moral code, so adherents would not excuse groups from general law.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Social harmony rests on conformity to ritual and role relationships, so eccentricity is not encouraged.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Not addressed; Mencius urges light burdens on the people, but nothing in the classics speaks to international debt.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Not addressed; Confucianism stresses livelihood and good rule, not who owns the economy under national independence.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Inferred: authority rests on the virtue of rulers and learned officials, not on assemblies elected to remake the constitution.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Confucians value order and a ruler's duty to secure livelihood, but also remonstrance and the right to remove a tyrant, so adherents are split.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Inferred: Confucian benevolence reaches beyond the family, though it is graded by closeness, so a duty to help distant poor is weaker than a duty to near ones.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Anachronistic; Mencius condemns aggressive war but accepts defence, so adherents have no settled view on nuclear weapons.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Inferred: rulers should be morally worthy and chosen for virtue, and the tradition is not built on popular election, though Mencius ties legitimacy to the people's acceptance.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Anachronistic; the classics address taxes and livelihood, not monetary institutions.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Not addressed; Mencius values peace and warns against conquest, but gives no rule on ceding land.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Inferred from Mencius, who makes securing the people's livelihood, as in the well-field system, the ruler's first duty, which places land use under a public purpose.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Anachronistic; Confucianism offers no basis for classifying the Soviet Union.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Mencius urges restraint in harvesting fish and timber so supplies last, from which care for uncertain future harm is inferred.

collective-defense.rationale: Not addressed in the classics; Mencius discusses small states serving larger ones and humane statecraft but not binding alliances.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Mencius says a conquest is justified only if the people welcome it, so annexation against the people's will is inferred to be illegitimate.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Confucianism has no church, and imperial governments supervised religious bodies; inferred from the moral primacy of the civil order.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The ruler is meant to be a moral exemplar for all the people, which is inferred to place him above faction.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Confucian tradition prizes unified rule under one legitimate order, so keeping a region is inferred as acceptable, though Mencius condemns unjust war.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Not addressed by the classics; adherents split between unity under one order and tolerating local custom.

sacred-ruler.rationale: The emperor was Son of Heaven, but the Mandate of Heaven makes his rule depend on virtue and Mencius treats a bad ruler as removable, so divine descent is not the basis of authority.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Mencius favours light taxes but the classics have no view on income-tax structure.

character-from-environment.rationale: The Analects hold that people are close by nature and far apart by practice, and Confucianism places moral cultivation through family, learning and ritual at its centre.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The ruler is bound by morality, ritual and the Mandate of Heaven, though Confucians stress virtue over law as the constraint.

space-expansion.rationale: Anachronistic and unaddressed; Confucianism's focus is on moral order in the human world.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Confucian thought places government in the hands of virtuous scholar-officials under a ruler and does not discuss mixing few and many.

leader-cult.rationale: The ruler is honoured through ritual but is held to moral standards, so mass glorification as the nation's embodiment is inferred to be foreign.

equal-parenting.rationale: Confucian role ethics assigns distinct duties to father and mother, so an equal-time presumption is inferred to be foreign to it.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Inferred from the Confucian stress on role harmony and moral rule from above, which has no place for class conflict as a motor of society.

land-redistribution.rationale: Mencius, in Teng Wen Gong I, calls for fair land division and the well-field system so every family has a livelihood.

refugee-return.rationale: Not addressed; benevolent rule is said to draw people to the ruler, but no right of return is stated.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Mencius counsels rulers against conquest and holds that authority comes from virtue, not from kinship or ethnic claim.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Confucianism coexisted with other teachings and has no doctrine of apostasy, so legal punishment is inferred to be foreign to it.

women-must-cover.rationale: Ritual stresses female modesty, but no state dress requirement is part of the doctrine; inferred.

common-currency.rationale: Not addressed; inferred only from its concern with livelihood and order, which does not settle currency union.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Inferred from its ideal of unified all-under-heaven rule by a virtuous king, which favours political unity of one cultural world.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Inferred from the imperial tradition of civilising outsiders through shared culture, which favours assimilation over separate institutions.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Not addressed; Confucius stresses duty to family and home order, but nothing settles minority strategy.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Mencius does say people without a livelihood lose moral steadiness, but he holds that the ruler's moral example drives order.

ban-cartels.rationale: Inferred from Mencius's concern that rulers secure the people's livelihood and from his criticism of those who monopolise gain.

no-bailouts.rationale: Not addressed; benevolent rulers relieve distress, but nothing is said about rescuing firms.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Confucianism has no theory of courts or majorities; it relies on virtuous officials, not on either, so adherents are split.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Husband-wife and ruler-subject roles are distinct in the five relationships, so equal quotas are not part of the tradition.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: In Teng Wen Gong I Mencius defends the division of labour and exchange against Xu Xing's self-sufficiency, so he rejects autarky.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Anachronistic; Mencius values prudent use of resources, but no trade standards are stated.

moral-incentives.rationale: Confucius holds that rulers and people should be led by virtue and ritual, not profit, and stresses duty over reward.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Mencius allows overthrowing a tyrant on Heaven's mandate, but only by a morally supported ruler responding to the people, not a small armed group.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The imperial tradition combined hereditary rule and rank with merit selection, so adherents would not simply abolish inherited privilege.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Confucian tradition treats the past and the sages of one's own civilization as the model for moral education, so history centred on it is inferred, though modern school curricula are not addressed.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Mencius speaks of using the doctrines of the Chinese to change barbarians, and the tradition holds that virtue transforms outsiders; formal rule over them is inferred only.

patriotic-education.rationale: Texts stress moral cultivation and loyalty to a virtuous ruler, but flags, anthems and national pride are modern and have no clear Confucian counterpart.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Racial preferences in admissions are far outside the texts, which care about merit and virtue but also about reciprocal duty; no settled view can be inferred.

public-money-creation.rationale: Money creation is not addressed; Mencius wants the ruler to secure livelihoods but proposes land and tax measures, not monetary institutions.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Capitalist crisis and collapse are not addressed in classical texts, and adherents have no common view.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Confucian ideal has virtuous rule attracting distant peoples and the imperial tradition kept a tributary order, so cultivating influence over former dependencies is inferred.

delink-world-market.rationale: Texts distrust profit-seeking but do not call for cutting ties with foreign states; poor-versus-rich country trade is an anachronistic question.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: The idea is Marxist and not addressed; Confucians care about livelihood and hierarchy of roles rather than class exploitation between nations.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Confucian ethics expects benevolence and reciprocal duties and values harmony over unrestricted private choice, so a right to refuse service on any grounds is inferred to be disliked.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Confucianism prefers rule by virtue and ritual to law, and the rights debate in the tradition is about whether rights fit it, so entrenched legal limits are inferred to be disfavoured.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: The doctrine does not address this; adherents take varied positions, so it is left neutral.

elective-rulers.rationale: Mencius ties legitimacy to Heaven's mandate shown by the people's acceptance and to the ruler's virtue, not to election; hereditary succession is accepted.

minority-veto.rationale: Order rests on hierarchy and the guidance of the virtuous, not on individual consent; inferred.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Mencius says a ruler who destroys benevolence and righteousness is a mere fellow who may be removed, and remonstrance is the first duty of officials.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The tradition has no parliament and puts rule in a virtuous sovereign advised by learned officials; inferred.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Mencius praises King Xuan's pity for a frightened ox as the heart that could carry him to benevolent rule.

animal-use-humane.rationale: In the same passage the ox is replaced by a sheep and the superior man keeps from the kitchen, accepting animal use while shunning cruelty.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Mencius makes caring for the destitute and the people's livelihood a ruler's first duty, and the cultivated are bound to serve the people.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Confucians hold that the cultivated should serve and reform the state, though one may withdraw when the Way does not prevail.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Confucians value ritual and music for shaping social order and see this as good, not as a critique.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Mencius contrasts the king who wins hearts by virtue with the hegemon who rules by force, and holds that the people's acceptance confers the mandate.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: The doctrine does not address this; adherents take varied positions, so it is left neutral.

native-born-offices.rationale: Offices go to the learned and virtuous through examination and merit, not birthplace; inferred.

party-own-road.rationale: The doctrine does not address this; adherents take varied positions, so it is left neutral.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: The doctrine does not address this; adherents take varied positions, so it is left neutral.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Mencius condemns wars of conquest and holds that benevolent rule wins people without war; demanding territory back is inferred to be disfavoured.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Rule is meant to go to the virtuous regardless of descent, so leadership by ancestry is inferred to be rejected.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Anachronistic; the ideology predates the question and never addressed it.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Anachronistic; the ideology predates the question and never addressed it.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: A historical question outside the ideology.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Reverence for ancestors and continuity of ritual suggests preserving inherited symbols; inferred.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: The doctrine does not address this; adherents take varied positions, so it is left neutral.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Reciprocal role duties exist but the ideology is patriarchal; adherents are split.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Stress on ritual, tradition and moral culture suggests institutions should grow from a civilization's own ethics; inferred, as modern political Confucianism is out of scope.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The tradition ranks civil learning and virtuous rule above force and condemns aggressive war; a political guardian role for the army is inferred to be rejected.

paid-care-work.rationale: Care for family is a filial and household duty, so treating it as paid labour is inferred to be foreign to the tradition.

missingStatements.text: Government should rely on the moral example of its rulers more than on laws and punishments.
missingStatements.rationale: Confucius holds that the ruler's virtue moves the people like wind bending grass, and Confucians wanted far less reliance on penal punishment.

missingStatements.text: A ruler who fails to care for the people may rightly be removed.
missingStatements.rationale: Mencius says a ruler who violates benevolence is a mere fellow who may be put to death and an evil ruler may be overthrown.

notes: Modern political Confucians split between meritocratic and constitutional-democratic proposals, so democracy-best and one-party-rule are left neutral. Legalist-influenced imperial practice and Xunzi would answer more authoritarian on law and punishment.
